name: Evernote
tagline: Note manager built on notebooks and tags, with a web clipper, scanning, and search inside attachments.
description: Evernote is a notebook-and-tag note manager built around capture: a web clipper, scanning, audio notes, and search that reads inside attachments.
pros: The web clipper captures full pages, articles, and screenshots straight into the notebook, per the note-taking comparison held in this repository
Search reaches inside attached documents and images, so a keyword can surface a PDF or a screenshot rather than only note titles
Notebooks plus tags give two independent ways to file the same material, which suits long-lived reference libraries
Capture spans text, scanned documents, audio notes, and clipped pages, keeping different source types on one shelf
Rated 4.2 out of 5 from 2,100 reviews in this repository's recorded data
cons: Structure is applied at filing time and stays put: tags do not map onto hierarchical tools, which is why the Notion review held in this repository records that migration as its hardest path

content.title: Notebooks, tags, and where clipping lands
content.body: Evernote's model is a filing one: notes live in notebooks, notebooks carry tags, and retrieval depends on both. The note-taking comparison in this repository calls it the most established dedicated note taking application and describes its organization as a notebook and tag system rather than a database or a linked graph. That decision has a consequence worth naming early: structure is applied when a note is filed, and it stays where it was put. The Notion review held in this repository records the same problem on the way out, noting that tags do not map onto a page hierarchy and that notebooks become pages rather than databases.

content.title: The web clipper as the capture path
content.body: The clipper is how most material gets in. This repository records a browser extension that captures full web pages, articles, and screenshots for offline reference, alongside text notes, document scanning, and audio notes. Capture is therefore where the product puts its weight: Evernote is bought to hold things found elsewhere, pages, PDFs, images, and meeting audio, and the notebook is the shelf they land on. Teams that live in links and reference material get the most from that shape, while teams producing their own documents usually keep drafting somewhere else.

content.title: Search that reads inside attachments
content.body: Retrieval is the counterweight to capture, and this is where the record is strongest. The same comparison describes Evernote's search as reaching inside attached documents and images, so a keyword can surface a PDF or a screenshot rather than only note titles. For a library built from clipping, that is the difference between a store and an archive anyone can use. The capture and retrieval surfaces recorded for the product are listed below.
items: Full-page and article capture from the browser
Audio notes kept in the same notebook
Search across attached documents and images
Tags and notebooks as the retrieval structure

content.title: What the free plan withholds
content.body: This page records Evernote as freemium with a band of $10-20/mo, which is the sole price this page carries. The note-taking comparison in this repository adds the shape of the free tier: it is limited to two devices, while paid plans remove the device restriction, add offline access, and raise attachment size limits. In practice the free tier is a trial of the capture habit rather than a durable home for it, because a third device or a flight without connectivity is where the limit first shows up.

content.title: What Evernote is not trying to be
content.body: Evernote is a store with a strong retrieval layer, not a linked thinking environment and not a shared workspace. Notes are filed rather than linked, so no graph of connections grows between them, and there is no block-level referencing that lets one passage appear in several places. This repository files the linked and local-first approaches under Roam Research and Obsidian, and databases plus pages under Notion. Buyers wanting a network of ideas should read those pages instead. Buyers wanting a searchable shelf of captured material are in the right place.

content.title: Sync, storage, and the certifications not on file
content.body: Evernote is a hosted service: notes sync across devices through the vendor's infrastructure, which is what makes multi-device access and clipping from any browser possible. The fields assembled for this review contain no certification entry for Evernote and nothing in that field is offered here; use the vendor’s current documentation as the source for that answer. Because a library like this tends to accumulate contracts, articles, and scanned documents, the questions worth asking are about how stored content is protected, how long deleted material is retained, and what export produces when the library leaves.

content.title: Notion, Obsidian, Roam, and the stray pairings
content.body: In this repository eleven comparison pages feature Evernote. Four are the ones that matter, Notion, Obsidian, Roam Research, and Todoist, where the argument is about organization and retrieval. The rest pair it with Calendly, Cal.com, Acuity Scheduling, JotForm, Typeform, Microsoft Teams, and ClickUp, which sell scheduling, forms, meetings, or project tracking, so those pages read as directory breadth rather than real rivalry.

content.title: Moving out of notebooks, as this repository records it
content.body: Migration is worth reading about before adoption rather than after. The Notion review in this repository rates importing a large Evernote library as the hardest of the import paths it describes, because tags have no counterpart in a page hierarchy, notebooks become pages instead of databases, and attachments lose their organizational context. The same logic runs in reverse: whatever a team chooses next, its structure should be settled before a decade of clipped pages are exported into it. A shelf is easy to fill and awkward to re-shelve.

content.title: Who should keep a notebook
content.body: Evernote fits researchers, analysts, and reference-heavy professionals whose material arrives from the web, from PDFs, and from meetings, and who value finding it again over linking it into anything. It fits individuals who want the same library on a phone, a laptop, and a browser. It does not fit teams that need shared live documents, or thinkers who want notes connected in a graph. This assessment is assembled from published product material and the entries this repository holds for Evernote; nobody on this page has worked inside an Evernote account. Those records show 4.2 out of 5 from 2,100 reviews.

faqs.question: How is Evernote organized?
faqs.answer: Notebooks and tags. The note-taking comparison in this repository describes Evernote as the most established dedicated note taking application, known for its notebook and tag organization system and search.

faqs.question: What does the Evernote web clipper capture?
faqs.answer: Full web pages, articles, and screenshots, recorded as saved for offline reference. Text notes, document scanning, and audio notes are recorded alongside it as the other capture types.

faqs.question: Can Evernote search inside PDFs and images?
faqs.answer: Yes, per this repository's comparison, which records search reaching within attached documents and images rather than stopping at note titles and tags.

faqs.question: What does Evernote's free plan limit?
faqs.answer: Two devices, according to the note-taking comparison held in this repository. Paid plans are recorded as removing the device restriction, adding offline access, and raising attachment size limits.

faqs.question: How does Evernote differ from Obsidian and Roam Research?
faqs.answer: Obsidian is a local-first Markdown vault with a graph of links; Roam is an outliner built on block references. Evernote is a notebook-and-tag store centered on capture and search.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Low for capture and filing; the judgment cost appears later, when notebooks and tags have to stay consistent across years of accumulated material
whoShouldUse: Researchers, analysts, and reference-heavy professionals whose material arrives from the web, from PDFs, and from meetings, and who care more about retrieving it than about linking it into a structure.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need shared live documents; thinkers who want notes connected in a graph; buyers who need a free tier across more than two devices, or a documented compliance record on file.
